# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Municipal air quality screening can identify widespread concern while offering limited spatial discrimination for control planning. We examined whether concentration patterns and source contributions provide additional management information in Congonhas, a mining-influenced municipality in southeastern Brazil. AERMOD outputs for 2021-2023, driven by a 2023 emissions inventory, were analysed at 1,008 municipal receptors from a regional network of 1,497 locations. Quintiles, clustering, correlograms and local Moran statistics were evaluated before results were linked to 311 zoning records through clipped Voronoi support. Annual global Moran statistics were 0.662 for PM~10~ and 0.754 for PM~2.5~, with 151 and 126 high-high receptors after conditional permutation and false-discovery adjustment. The four-indicator reference favoured Ward with two groups and silhouette 0.533. A complementary six-indicator analysis, including hourly and daily maxima and annual means, favoured k-means with two groups and silhouette 0.481. The complete-meteorology reference used 24,892 valid hours and 1,075 eligible days. Restricting daily analysis to 463 persistent-direction days omitted higher maxima at 574 PM~10~ and 749 PM~2.5~ municipal receptors. Spatially blocked emission-concentration screening produced incomplete associations and did not identify a universal allowable emission threshold. Relative regionalization distinguished receiving priorities from source-control needs, while temporal and neighbourhood tests exposed conditions affecting the classification. These results support targeted investigation and zoning communication without removing model bias or establishing ambient attainment.

Keywords regionalization, spatial autocorrelation, source attribution, land-use planning, mining.
